answer:
The claim is directly supported by multiple pieces of evidence:

- Scanned, image-only PDFs lack an embedded text layer; without OCR, the standard parser extracts zero text, and citations cannot be generated [NL-006#NL-006-S03].
- In support tickets, scanned PDFs without a text layer cause TutorChat to either return an answer with no source citations because it cannot find text offsets, or to point to the entire document (e.g., page 1 of a 250-page PDF) instead of a specific section [NL-021#NL-021-S02].
- At BrightPath Healthcare, ~60% of clinical documentation is scanned, image-only PDFs; for those files, citation mapping still fails—either pointing to page one of a 200-page document or generating no citation link at all, such as the code blue checklist that pointed to page 1 instead of page 87 [NL-018#NL-018-S04].
- The remaining citation tickets in May and June 2026 were almost entirely linked to scanned, image-only PDFs; TutorChat struggles to establish citation anchors, often linking back to the start of the file rather than the specific page [NL-011#NL-011-S05].
- A low-resolution scanned PDF can produce a correct answer but "No citation available" because the layout parser cannot determine the exact page or section ID [NL-006#NL-006-S04].
- User-facing documentation states that low-quality scanned PDFs may struggle to generate page-specific citations due to OCR limitations [NL-028#NL-028-S03].
- Product/design discussions propose warning users at upload that scanned/image-only files ingested without OCR "may result in poor citation quality," and an Admin Console example flags a scanned PDF as showing only 45% citation confidence [NL-021#NL-021-S05].
- OCR is heuristic; blurry, low-resolution, or complex-layout scans can produce misreads and broken paragraphs, directly causing broken citations and gaps in knowledge [NL-006#NL-006-S03].
